headline: AI data center power demand is the new bottleneck, with US grid connection waits of two years driving hyperscalers to seek alternative on-site power solutions
reasoning: Matt Dever argues that after two years of GPU supply being the primary AI bottleneck, the constraint has shifted to power grid capacity. The IEA reported a 50% rise in AI data center electricity consumption in 2025, illustrating the scale of demand. In the US, grid connection wait times are now two years, pushing hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta to pursue behind-the-meter, on-site power generation. Alternative technologies such as fuel cells and nuclear SMRs are gaining traction due to faster deployment timelines. China is noted to have a comparative advantage given overcapacity built in renewables over the past decade.
quote: we've for the last two years, we've we've had what we would see as a bit of a bottleneck in terms of GPUs and the the underlying, um, mechanics of the, the AI transition. But really now it's come down to that, that power grid, and we see that as, as the new bottleneck. So to give you a good example, the the International Energy Agency, uh, in 2025 said that AI data center electricity consumption rose by 50%. So that gives you an indication of of how strong and the huge demand that we're seeing from from these data centers. Now, how how companies alleviate that problem is, is the the biggest thing in the US. You've got a two year wait for for grid connection.
episode_title: The electrifying plays powering the AI trade

headline: Gas will play a necessary role in powering AI data centers despite renewables being the preferred long-term solution, given renewable lead times
reasoning: Dever acknowledges that while renewables are the preferred sustainability outcome, their long lead times make them impractical as a near-term power solution for AI data centers. Gas is identified as a likely bridging energy source even though it is not ideal. The key competitive advantage lies in speed-to-market power delivery, with hyperscalers seeking on-site solutions to bypass grid constraints.
quote: in an ideal world, we'd like to see that that power get drawn from renewables, because we see that as, as the way forward in terms of sustainability. But that's not always that's not always possible. And given the lead times in, in the traditional renewable area, then you know that that becomes difficult. So I think gas is gas is certainly going to be a part of it. Now that's that's not ideal. But ultimately looking at so the the winners, the bottlenecks and the essentially the capital pits. So who can who can access the quickest to market if you like power source.
episode_title: The electrifying plays powering the AI trade

headline: Emit Capital holds Vertiv as a core AI infrastructure position, citing strong revenue growth and critical cooling and power management exposure
reasoning: Dever notes Emit Capital holds Vertiv across 35 portfolios, indicating it is a broad core position. The stock suffered a significant drawdown in July 2024 before rebounding to around $293-$300. Q2 revenue was up 24% with approximately $3.3 billion in revenue growth. Vertiv's investment case centres on its diversification across power management and particularly cooling services, which are essential for AI data centres. Dever frames this as an infrastructure-side play rather than a direct power generation bet.
quote: vertically is one of those stocks that has a huge tailwind. We see from from the demand. And it's more on the infrastructure side. So it's not it's not looking at it from the power side. But obviously we saw a we saw a significant drop there in July, which wasn't uncommon when it comes to to the AI sector. But um, it's obviously rebounded, you know, quite significantly since and I think it's traded around 300 or around 293 at the moment. So, you know, it's Q2 revenue was was up 24%. So it's earnings results are significant. I think there was around 3.3 billion in terms of revenue growth. So vertex is one of those particularly when you look at their diversification of services. So power management, um, but also probably more importantly is their the cooling side of their business, which, which tends to, um, tends to be significant when you look at the AI sector.

headline: Emit Capital is a long-term holder of Bloom Energy, viewing its solid oxide fuel cells as the fastest path to on-site data centre power and a significant rerating opportunity
reasoning: Dever has held Bloom Energy for a long time and expresses high confidence in its technology and commercialisation trajectory. Bloom Energy's solid oxide fuel cells can be deployed on-site for data centres, bypassing the two-year US grid connection backlog — Oracle deployed the technology in just 55 days. The client base now includes Oracle, Apple, Google, Walmart and AEP, demonstrating commercial validation. Dever acknowledges it is patient capital with risks attached, but sees meaningful valuation upside as the technology scales beyond the US. He explicitly identifies Bloom as the type of company that addresses the power bottleneck constraining AI infrastructure build-out.
